claim: std::fs is a module, not a trait or interface, so there is no way to substitute a mock filesystem for it in Rust unit tests.
stance_target: ha-linux-agent cannot rely on filesystem mocking for unit tests and must use another strategy (temp dirs or trait abstraction)
quoted_support: All the fs access in Rust is built on top of std::fs which is a module, not a trait or any other kind of interface, so there is no real way to substitute std::fs by std::mock_fs or something like that for the tests.

claim: The community-endorsed approach for fs-touching Rust tests is the tempfile crate's tempdir, which auto-deletes on scope exit and defaults to the OS temp directory (usually tmpfs/ramdisk on Linux).
stance_target: ha-linux-agent's file-walking/reading code can be tested hermetically with tempfile instead of mocking or relying on host state
quoted_support: You might want to try the tempfile crate ... With that you can create individual files or directories, and they will be deleted when the object goes out of scope. I think the crate also defaults to using the OS's designated temporary directories, e.g. /tmp/ on linux, which is usually a tmpfs/ramdisk.

claim: An alternative testability strategy is abstracting over the std Read/Write/Seek traits that std::fs::File implements, allowing fake I/O in unit tests.
stance_target: ha-linux-agent can architect file-reading code against std I/O traits so unit tests need no real filesystem at all
quoted_support: Alternatively, the types from std::fs implement several traits over which you might be able to abstract, e.g. Read, Write, Seek.
